# How a Heat Pump Works

Think of a heat pump as a heat mover, not a heat maker. That single idea is the key to understanding the whole thing.

When you burn gas or run an electric heater, you're *creating* heat. A heat pump does something different: it takes heat that already exists somewhere and moves it somewhere else. That's why it can be so efficient. You're not generating energy from nothing; you're just relocating it.

## The Basic Trick

Here's a simple analogy. Imagine you have a sponge. You can soak it up in a puddle, then wring it out somewhere else. A heat pump does the same thing with heat, except instead of a sponge, it uses a special fluid called a **refrigerant**.

Refrigerant has a useful property: it boils at very low temperatures. At normal room temperature, a refrigerant can turn from liquid to gas. And here's the magic part — when any liquid turns into a gas, it absorbs heat from its surroundings. That's exactly why sweat cools your skin. The liquid evaporates, and in doing so, it pulls heat away from your body.

## The Four Parts

A heat pump has four main components that work together in a loop:

**1. Evaporator (outside coil):** The refrigerant arrives here as a cold, low-pressure liquid. Because it's colder than the outside air — even when it's freezing out — it absorbs heat from that air. As it absorbs heat, it boils and turns into a gas. Yes, even at -10°C, there's still heat energy in the air. The refrigerant soaks it up.

**2. Compressor:** This is the heart of the system. The compressor squeezes that low-pressure gas into a much smaller space. When you compress a gas, it heats up. Think of how a bicycle pump gets warm when you use it. The compressor does this to the refrigerant, raising its temperature well above what's inside your house.

**3. Condenser (inside coil):** Now the hot, high-pressure gas flows through coils inside your home. Because the gas is hotter than the air in your rooms, it gives off its heat. As it releases that heat, it condenses back into a liquid. A fan blows air over these coils, distributing the warmth through your house.

**4. Expansion valve:** The liquid refrigerant is still under high pressure. It passes through a tiny opening — the expansion valve — where the pressure drops suddenly. This causes it to cool dramatically, ready to go back outside and absorb more heat.

Then the cycle repeats, over and over, hundreds of times per hour.

## Heating and Cooling

Most heat pumps can run in reverse. In summer, you flip a switch (a reversing valve), and the whole process flips direction. Now the indoor coil acts as the evaporator, pulling heat *out* of your house and dumping it outside. Your house becomes the cold side, and the outside becomes the hot side. Same system, opposite direction.

## Why It's Efficient

A gas furnace might deliver one unit of heat for every unit of fuel you burn. A heat pump can deliver three or four units of heat for every unit of electricity used to run the compressor. Why? Because most of that heat isn't created by the electricity — it's free heat pulled from the outside air. The electricity just powers the moving parts.

That's the whole idea. No combustion, no flame. Just a refrigerant doing what liquids and gases naturally do, guided by a compressor, shuttling heat from one place to another.
